title: Do you need a mouse with an 8K polling rate?
summary: A gaming mouse with an 8,000 Hz polling rate sounds awesome and speedy on paper, but let's take a look at what that actually means.
body: For years, the standard polling rate for gaming peripherals — mice, keyboards, etc. — has been 1,000 Hz, which equates to a delay, or latency, of 1 millisecond. This is significantly higher than the standard polling rate for non-gaming peripherals, by the way, which is 125 Hz (8ms latency) — in fact, it's eight times as fast. Well, over the last couple of years, gaming companies have been asking: What if we made the polling rate even faster than 1,000 Hz? What if we made it eight times as fast? And now just about every single ultra-lightweight, esports-oriented gaming mouse that comes out has up to an 8,000 Hz polling rate. And, of course, this raises the question every time: Do you actually need a mouse with an 8,000 Hz polling rate? And the answer is... probably not. What is polling rate, and what does it mean? Polling rate is, simply put, how often your mouse communicates with your PC. That is, how often it reports mouse movement and clicks to your CPU. At a standard gaming mouse polling rate of 1,000 Hz, your mouse is communicating with your PC 1,000 times per second — or, once every millisecond. Hence, a 1,000 Hz polling rate means 1ms latency. body: Wi-Fi is great until you hit lag, network congestion, or interference. If you need to expand your network, you'll want a network switch with gigabit speeds. Luckily, Amazon's big sale means you can pick up this TP-Link Lightwave 5-port unmanaged Ethernet switch for just $7.99 right now , bringing it back down to its lowest-ever price. ● Check out this deal on Amazon With the LS1005G, you're getting five extra Ethernet ports for your network, although you'll need to use one to connect it to your existing router. There isn't a better option than an Ethernet cable for maxing out the bandwidth on your internet connection, especially if you prefer to stream or play games online. Gigabit speeds shouldn't seem that exciting these days, but plenty of people are rocking old network hardware that isn't this fast. You don't need to worry about Wi-Fi lag or interference here, as you'll get a solid, dedicated wired connection instead. There's no need to think about a setup process either, as the LS1005G is completely unmanaged. You just need to plug it in, hooking your router up to the switch's WAN port. title: Get a Wi-Fi 7 mesh network for a discounted $149.99 — TP-Link Deco 7 BE25 offers 5,012 Mbps speeds and coverage for 150 devices
summary: TP-Link’s Deco 7 BE25 combines Wi-Fi 7 speeds, wide coverage, 2.5Gbps Ethernet, and support for 150-plus devices in a mesh system that now costs considerably less.
body: If you're looking to upgrade your home network without spending a fortune, investing in a mesh Wi-Fi 7 system is worth considering. Combining fast wireless speeds with wide-area coverage, it is a practical option for homes with multiple devices, including smartphones, gaming PCs, laptops, smart TVs, and smart home devices. Currently on sale, the TP-Link Deco 7 BE25 BE500 mesh Wi-Fi 7 dual-pack is currently available for $149.99 on Amazon , down from its selling price of $199.99. If you want even wider coverage, the triple pack is also on sale and can be purchased for $198.19 , which is over $100 off its listed price of $299.99. Check out the TP-Link Deco 7 BE25 BE500 mesh Wi-Fi 7 dual-pack on Amazon Check out the TP-Link Deco 7 BE25 BE500 mesh Wi-Fi 7 triple-pack on Amazon Built around dual-band Wi-Fi 7, the TP-Link Deco 7 BE25 mesh system offers combined speeds of up to 5,012 Mbps. It can reach up to 4,324 Mbps on the 5 GHz band and 688 Mbps on 2.4 GHz, making it suitable for demanding workloads such as 4K streaming, online gaming, and AR/VR applications. title: Florida sues TP-Link for ‘lying about the safety of its routers’
summary: Florida and three other states have sued the company on the grounds that it's misleading their citizens about the security of its products and its ties with China.
body: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier just announced that the state is suing TP-Link, claiming that the company has been “lying about the safety of its routers and its ties to the CCP.” Uthmeier posted a minute-and-a-half video clip on X, saying that TP-Link’s claims of having safe routers aren’t true. Today, we sued TP-Link for lying about the safety of its routers and its ties to the CCP.TP-Link sold Floridians the digital front door to their home network while misrepresenting how secure it was, how separated the company was from China, and what could happen to their data. https://t.co/Hg3czpNvEV October 6, 2026 “Chinese state-sponsored hackers exploited TP-Link routers sitting in American living rooms. Many of those models cannot even update themselves automatically, and TP-Link has stopped supporting them,” the Florida AG said on the social media platform. “They also told Floridians they have split from China and that they build U.S. products in Vietnam, but that is fiction. Research and manufacturing remain rooted in China, less than 1% of the parts in that Vietnam plant actually come from Vietnam.
